title: Genomic Medicine and Precision Therapeutics
answer: Polygenic risk, gene editing design, pharmacogenomics, epigenetic age and rare disease diagnosis.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Polygenic Risk Scores
children.blurb: Polygenic risk scores are numbers that summarise the combined effect of many small genetic variants on the chance of developing a condition such as coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes or breast cancer.

children.name: Gene Editing Guide Design
children.blurb: Gene editing guide design is the work of choosing the RNA sequence and delivery format that will direct an editing tool to one intended site in a genome and few others.

children.name: Pharmacogenomics
children.blurb: Pharmacogenomics is the study of how inherited genetic variation changes a person's response to a drug, covering both how the body processes a medicine and how the medicine acts on its target.

children.name: Epigenetic Aging Clocks
children.blurb: Epigenetic aging clocks are models that estimate biological age from DNA methylation patterns measured across selected sites in the genome.

children.name: Rare Disease Diagnosis
children.blurb: Rare disease diagnosis covers the use of computational methods to identify conditions that individually affect few people but collectively are common, often after a long diagnostic odyssey.

sections.body: Genomic medicine uses a person's DNA to guide prevention, diagnosis and treatment, and artificial intelligence has become a working tool in several parts of that pipeline. Polygenic risk scores combine thousands of common variants into a single number, and machine learning models are used to build and validate those scores across biobank cohorts. In gene editing, models predict guide RNA efficiency and off target activity before any lab work begins, which narrows the candidate list for CRISPR experiments. Pharmacogenomics uses learned models to link variants in drug metabolising enzymes to likely drug response. Epigenetic clocks estimate biological age from DNA methylation patterns, and neural networks have improved how well those clocks track health outcomes. Rare disease diagnosis is where AI is most visibly deployed, with phenotype matching and variant prioritisation tools shortening the diagnostic odyssey for families.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The field is uneven. Polygenic scores work reasonably well for traits with strong polygenic architecture in populations represented in the training data, and they transfer poorly to other ancestries, which is a known and unresolved limitation. Guide design models are useful ranking tools but no model removes the need for experimental validation, and off target prediction remains imperfect. Pharmacogenomic associations for a small set of genes are well established and clinically actionable, while most of the genome is not. Epigenetic clocks correlate with age and mortality risk but the causal story is contested, and a clock reading is not a diagnosis. Rare disease tools depend on the quality of phenotype terms entered by clinicians, and they produce candidate lists rather than answers. Across all five areas, the recurring limits are data representation, ancestry bias, and the gap between statistical association and clinical utility.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here trace a path from population level risk to individual diagnosis. Polygenic Risk Scores covers how many small effects are aggregated and where that aggregation breaks down, and it sets up the statistical thinking used elsewhere in the section. Gene Editing Guide Design moves from reading genomes to writing them, covering the models that score guides and predict off target edits. Pharmacogenomics sits between genetics and prescribing, explaining how variants in drug metabolism genes are matched to medications. Epigenetic Aging Clocks deals with methylation data and the models that turn it into an age estimate, including what that estimate does and does not mean. Rare Disease Diagnosis is the clinical endpoint, where phenotype and genotype data are combined to surface candidate conditions. A reader new to the area would start with polygenic scores for the statistical foundation, then move to rare disease diagnosis to see the clinical payoff, and use the other three pages for the specific methods they need.
